Upon hatching, the newly emerged chick weighs approximately 54.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 54.5 grams], a mass that reflects the substantial yolk reserves and the energetic investment made by the parents during the incubation period. This neonatal weight marks the beginning of a rapid growth trajectory that demands a steady supply of lipid-rich forage fish delivered by both attending adults. Field studies on Protection Island indicate that chicks that fledge with a lower body mass often experience reduced post-fledging survival, underscoring the importance of this initial condition. The nestling period is characterized by intense parental provisioning, with adults commuting long distances to productive feeding grounds. The thermal environment of the burrow, which remains near 36 °C, facilitates efficient embryonic development and early growth, while also protecting the chick from the cooler maritime air temperatures typical of the Pacific Northwest.

This delay between fledging and sexual maturity is a common life-history pattern among long-lived seabirds, allowing juveniles ample time to develop the foraging proficiency and body condition necessary to support the high energetic costs of reproduction.

The first successful breeding event for a rhinoceros auklet typically occurs at 1,095 days after hatching [tR = 1,095 days after hatching] under the typical body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], representing a significant delay between the attainment of sexual maturity and the onset of actual parental investment. This deferred first reproduction is likely driven by the competitive nature of their breeding colonies, where established individuals occupy the most favorable burrow sites, and younger birds must compete for limited nesting locations. A female will then produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and, in most years, will attempt just one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year], a conservative reproductive strategy that prioritizes the survival of the individual over high annual fecundity. This low reproductive rate, combined with their extended period to first breeding, places the species firmly on the slow end of the life-history continuum. Such a strategy is energetically feasible only because of the rich, predictable marine food resources available in their cold-water habitats, which support the high metabolic demands of both the provisioning adult and the rapidly growing nestling.

By the time a rhinoceros auklet reaches its maximum adult size, it attains a body mass of 544.1 grams [Wwi = 544.1 grams], a value that represents the culmination of an extended growth phase following the fledging period. This ultimate wet weight is considerably larger than that of many other alcids, reflecting the species' relatively robust body plan, which is adapted for efficient underwater propulsion during pursuit diving. Long-term mark-recapture studies from colonies in the Gulf of Alaska have documented that the maximum lifespan of this species can reach 28.2 years [am = 28.2 years] when measured at a core body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], a longevity that is consistent with their slow reproductive pace and high annual adult survival rates. This extended lifespan allows individuals to compensate for their low annual fecundity over many breeding seasons, thereby achieving a lifetime reproductive output that sustains stable populations. The physiological mechanisms underlying this longevity likely include efficient antioxidant defense systems and a relatively low mass-specific metabolic rate compared to terrestrial birds of similar body mass, traits that are commonly observed among pelagic seabirds.

The annual reproductive strategy of the rhinoceros auklet is closely tied to the seasonal productivity of the marine environment, with the timing of egg-laying pulsed to coincide with the peak abundance of forage fish like sand lance and Pacific herring. A detailed comparison with the closely related Cassin's auklet reveals that the rhinoceros auklet's slower pace of life, evident in its smaller clutch size and longer development times, is compensated by its greater body size and higher per-offspring provisioning capacity. During the non-breeding season, these birds disperse widely across the North Pacific, and significant variation in winter oceanographic conditions can influence the body condition of returning adults. Foraging ecology studies using geolocator tags have shown that individuals exhibit strong fidelity to specific wintering areas, which may affect their subsequent breeding success. The species' reliance on a narrow thermal niche around 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C] for basic physiological processes underscores its vulnerability to rising ocean temperatures, which could disrupt the timing of prey availability and the energetic balance between foraging effort and chick provisioning demands.
